subtitle: Supermarket quantities, fashion choices, sensory descriptions, and safe online ordering

stories.title: A Fresh Food Market Flyer
stories.summary: The printed Fresh Food Market flyer, kept word-for-word: the bakery, meat and poultry, and greengrocer paragraphs.
stories.narrative: A. At FFM’s (Fresh Food Market), you can find a great selection of delicious and tempting cakes and desserts. Choose from fresh cream cakes and fruit flans to tasty pastries and delicious muffins – many prepared in-store. The boxes of doughnuts include a range of tempting flavours. For any special occasion there’s a great range of celebration cakes too! B. Every FFM has well trained butchers in-store, able to prepare over a hundred cuts of meat like beef and lamb ribs, pork chops and steaks. So whether it’s some mince for a cottage pie or a turkey for a special occasion, our butcher can prepare the cut that’s right for you. C. At FFM’s we carefully select and pack most of the fresh fruit and vegetables. You always find a superb selection of ready prepared salads and pre-washed vegetables. FFM offers a variety of organic products such as eggs, cheese, potatoes, mushrooms, tea bags and muesli that don’t cost the earth. We are always on hand to help you with your selection.

stories.title: A Choice at the Department Store
stories.summary: A short reading profile about choosing a gift at a department store and describing its colour, material and fit.
stories.narrative: A girl visits a department store to find a Father’s Day present. The class fashion-show activity asks pupils to walk like fashion models on the catwalk. Its table gives two examples: a cute, pink sweater and smart, dark blue, denim jeans. The official word list spells the sweater material woolen, while the Pupil’s Book table prints woollen. The table also lists the adjectives baggy, tight and loose, the elegant material silk, and items including a skirt, a sweater and a track suit. The material column includes cotton, and one table sentence says, “They match his T-shirt.” Before the listening, pupils look at receipts from different shops and choose one item as a present. The black shirt costs $30.95, and its colour does not suit the girl’s father, so it is too expensive. She chooses the green cotton T-shirt because it feels soft and matches his linen jacket.

stories.title: A Safe Toy Order
stories.summary: A short project profile about choosing toys for pupils in Cyprus without submitting a real order.
stories.narrative: John and Mary are choosing toys for pupils in Cyprus. They read an online site and write down each item, the unit price, the quantity, the subtotal and the total. A space shuttle toy is only one item in the selection. For extra practice, the teacher can also ask pupils to stay within a budget. They must check the information with a parent and must not send the order. The project helps them organise numbers, compare choices and make a safe decision.

grammar_lab.title: Shopping Grammar Lab: Quantity, Senses, and Adjectives
grammar_lab.theme: At the supermarket, at the mall, and online
target_structures: a / an, some, any, how much, how many
Verbs of the senses: look, feel, taste, smell, sound
a few / few and a little / little
Order of adjectives: opinion, colour, material, item
Order form: unit price × quantity = subtotal

rules.usage: Countable nouns have a singular and plural form. Uncountable nouns have one form and are measured with words such as some, much and a little.

rules.concept: some, any, how much and how many
rules.usage: Use some in affirmative sentences. Use any in negative and question sentences. Use how many with plural countable nouns and how much with uncountable nouns.
examples: How many boxes do we need?
How much milk do we need?

rules.usage: Use look, feel, taste, smell and sound with like to ask about a thing's appearance, touch, taste, smell or sound.

rules.concept: a few / few and a little / little
rules.usage: Use a few before plural countable nouns and a little before uncountable nouns when there is enough. Use few or little when there is not enough.
In the book pattern, put an opinion word first, then a colour, then a material, and then the item.

practice_items.explanation: Milk is uncountable, so use some in an affirmative sentence.
Apples are countable, so ask how many.

practice_items.sentence: There is ____ bread in the bag.
practice_items.explanation: Bread is uncountable, so use a little.
We use feel for how a thing feels when touched.

practice_items.sentence: The subtotal is the cost of one line before the ____.
practice_items.explanation: The subtotal comes before the final total.

classroom_listening.title: At the Department Store: A Father's Day Gift

dialogue_script.speaker: Man
dialogue_script.text: Hi young lady. How may I help you?

dialogue_script.speaker: Girl
dialogue_script.text: Well... yeah. I’m looking for a Father’s Day gift.

dialogue_script.speaker: Man
dialogue_script.text: OK. How about getting your father a new shirt?

dialogue_script.speaker: Girl
dialogue_script.text: Hmm. That’s a good idea.

dialogue_script.speaker: Man
dialogue_script.text: What size does he take?

dialogue_script.speaker: Girl
dialogue_script.text: Well… I’m not sure.

dialogue_script.speaker: Man
dialogue_script.text: What does he look like?

dialogue_script.speaker: Girl
dialogue_script.text: He’s tall with broad shoulders and hmm…I think he is getting a little overweight now.

dialogue_script.speaker: Man
dialogue_script.text: Extra large, then. Look at this black one. Do you think it fits him?

dialogue_script.speaker: Girl
dialogue_script.text: That’s all right but the colour doesn’t suit him. He’s rather dark. I think the striped one suits him better. How much is it, anyway?

dialogue_script.speaker: Man
dialogue_script.text: Oh. It’s only $30.95.

dialogue_script.speaker: Girl
dialogue_script.text: Huh? That’s too expensive for me. Do you have something cheaper?

dialogue_script.speaker: Man
dialogue_script.text: Hmm. How about this green T-shirt? It’s pure cotton.

dialogue_script.speaker: Girl
dialogue_script.text: Umm...it feels so soft and I think my father likes this design. It matches his linen jacket, but the price tag says $13.99, and I know I don’t have that much money. I only have $12, 00.

dialogue_script.speaker: Man
dialogue_script.text: Well, let me see… You’re lucky. This T-shirt just went on sale. It’s only $11.90. What do you say?

dialogue_script.speaker: Girl
dialogue_script.text: Oh, thanks. I’ll take it.

paragraphs.heading: Recipients and purpose
paragraphs.guiding_questions: Who will receive the order? Why is the order being planned? Is this a real purchase or a practice task?
paragraphs.sample_starter: This practice order is for pupils in a primary school in Cyprus. It is a school project, so we will not send it.

paragraphs.heading: Choose and describe items
paragraphs.guiding_questions: Which items do you choose? What is each item? Which details help another pupil understand it?
paragraphs.sample_starter: First, we choose a small toy. The toy is light, safe and suitable for the age group.

paragraphs.heading: Unit prices and quantities
paragraphs.guiding_questions: What is the unit price? How many items do you need? How do you calculate each subtotal?
paragraphs.sample_starter: The unit price is written on the order form. We multiply it by the quantity to calculate the subtotal.

paragraphs.heading: Total and safety check
paragraphs.guiding_questions: What is the final total? Who should check the order with you? How can you shop safely online?
paragraphs.sample_starter: Finally, we add the subtotals to find the total. We check the information with a parent and never send the practice order.

teacher_notes.title: Pending: pair of snickers
teacher_notes.note: The source prints “pair of snickers” and “a pair of snickers” in the writing task. The likely intended forms are “pair of sneakers” and “a pair of sneakers”. The app keeps the printed headword, but the app gloss now uses the intended shoe sense instead of the false chocolate-bar reading; full headword replacement still needs teacher approval.

teacher_notes.title: Pending: unit pice
teacher_notes.note: The source word list prints “unit pice”, while the order form prints “Unit Price”. The app keeps the printed list form until the teacher approves “unit price”.

teacher_notes.title: Pending: woolen
teacher_notes.note: The source word list prints “woolen”; the Pupil’s Book word bank prints “woollen”. The app keeps the list form until the teacher approves the British-English spelling.

teacher_notes.title: Pending: a dozen of eggs
teacher_notes.note: The book prints “a dozen of eggs”. Standard English normally uses “a dozen eggs”. Workbook checks will accept both forms only after the teacher approves this policy.

teacher_notes.title: Pending: cider on a birthday list
teacher_notes.note: The source lists “20 cans of cider” in a child’s birthday-party list. The app leaves the printed quantity unchanged and does not present alcohol as a treat for pupils.

teacher_notes.title: Pending: Off the oven
teacher_notes.note: The model poem prints “Off the oven”. The likely model is “Out of the oven” or “Fresh from the oven”; the app keeps the printed wording pending teacher approval.

teacher_notes.title: Missing Internet-site image content
teacher_notes.note: The extracted source does not contain the toy names, prices or assembly-piece count from the printed website. The project uses a safe, blank order-form model and does not invent those values.

teacher_notes.title: Space shuttle is a toy in this unit
teacher_notes.note: The source uses a space shuttle toy on a website. The app does not present the historical Space Shuttle programme as current; the last shuttle flight was in 2011.

teacher_notes.title: Visual gloss opportunity
teacher_notes.note: Fruit flans are an explicit teacher example for a visual gloss. The vocabulary record includes image_prompt, but no picture is shipped until the teacher selects and reviews one.

teacher_notes.title: Pound as weight and money
teacher_notes.note: The book places “2 pounds of pork chops” beside “£1 = 100p”. The app teaches pound as a weight and as money without treating the two senses as the same item.

teacher_notes.title: Pending (E7): extracted key repeats d
teacher_notes.note: The extracted Teacher’s Book key uses d for blanks 2 and 6, while the dialogue structure suggests c for the price question. No key correction is applied.

teacher_notes.title: Pending (E8): key wording mismatch
teacher_notes.note: The printed e-mail says ‘quite tall’ and ‘dark T-shirts’, while the extracted key says ‘rather tall’ and ‘dark bright T-shirts’. The app follows the printed e-mail and records the mismatch.

teacher_notes.title: Pending (E9): extracted key order
teacher_notes.note: The extracted key appears to swap the answers for some butter and any milk. The app keeps the book activity and records the contradiction for teacher review.

teacher_notes.title: Pending (E10): beer in a primary exercise
teacher_notes.note: The printed B4 item uses ‘beer’. The app preserves the exercise and does not recommend it as a pupil shopping example until the teacher decides whether to annotate or replace it.

teacher_notes.title: Source limitation: Greek sign layout
teacher_notes.note: The extracted Greek supermarket-sign layout is incomplete. The app uses the Teacher’s Book key meanings, labels the limitation, and does not invent missing sign text.

teacher_notes.title: Pending (E11): printed $12, 00
teacher_notes.note: The extracted script prints “$12, 00”. The app keeps that verbatim recording text pending teacher approval; standard price punctuation would be $12.00.

book_checks.title: Teacher decision pending
book_checks.note: E1-E11 remain pending. The app preserves the printed forms and does not silently correct them.
